stage.byline: By Michelle Pera-McGhee and David Mora

text.value: To find out, we gathered every Billboard top-20 hit since 1958, [7,300] songs, and found their chord progressions on popular online chord sites.
But to compare thousands of songs, we first need a way to tell when two of them are doing the same thing.
Underneath the melody is a song’s harmony, a bed of chords (multiple notes played together) that shift in a repeating pattern called a chord progression.
But the literal chord names you might be familiar with – like C, D, or E – miss something important.
“Let It Be”, “Don’t Stop Believin’”, and “Wagon Wheel” all have different chords on paper.
But to your ear, they move in the same way.
Rotate the circles, and you can see that these progressions all take the same shape.
Every song has a key, a home base chord that it keeps returning to. If we name each chord by its distance from home, we can see that these songs actually share a chord progression.
Musicians notate this with roman numerals. The I is the home base chord, ii is a step away, iii is another step away, so on and so forth.
Click any chord to flip between its name and numeral.
So, we can describe all of these progressions as I-V-vi-IV.
Basically, you could sing the beginning of “Don’t Stop Believin’” over any of these, and it would sound right.
This is what we’ll call the axis of awesome progression.
Songs also differ in how much they lean on a progression. Some are 100% one progression on repeat. Others use it as one ingredient in a more varied harmonic recipe.
With those two ideas, which progressions a song uses and how much, we can put every song on the same map.
Each dot is a song, placed near songs that use a similar mix of chord progressions. When enough similar songs gather in one area, they form a cluster. This is the axis of awesome cluster.
They were onto something, lots of songs rely heavily on this progression, but this only makes up about [3%] of songs in the dataset.
<span class=small>Hear some below by clicking on the dots! Only select songs labeled with 🎧 are playable.
Let’s zoom out. Here are all [7,000] Billboard top-20 hits going back to 1958.

These colored clusters are concentrated similar songs, labeled by their main chord progression. Songs in grey don't have enough close neighbors to belong to any cluster; their mix of progressions is too unusual.

The map has no axes, so being at the top or on the left doesn't mean anything. What matters is what's nearby: songs that sit close together use similar progressions. Two clusters on opposite sides of the map aren't necessarily more different than two that are a little apart.
Learn more about how we matched chord progressions and made the map in the methods.
Let’s take a tour.
[Down here], we find the imagine cluster, with lots of songs that use I-IV-I-IV, like “Imagine” or “Walk On The Wild Side.”
Over here is another large cluster, la bamba.
This is a classic progression used across many genres, like rock, blues, and pop.
Here’s free fallin.
So far, visiting the biggest clusters, we’ve only seen the chords I, IV, and V.
I, IV, and V are the most common in these hits, making up [52%] of all chords across all songs.
If you’re gonna learn 3 chords, learn those.
There’s a reason. These are the 3 core building blocks of Western harmony that create a journey of tension and release. This goes way back, like Bach back.
The I is home base. It feels stable and resolved.
The IV creates gentle movement away from home.
The V creates tension and expectation. It really wants to go back to the I.
Like in “You’re Still The One” by Shania Twain, where it ends on the V. My ear, at least, is waiting for it to finally return home to the I.

axis of awesome throws the vi in there too, which shares two of its three notes with the I. So when the V sets you up to go home, you land somewhere that almost feels like home, and the loop continues.
These four chords (the “four chords”) show up again and again on this map, just sometimes in a different order.
For example, shivers takes the four chords (I-V-vi-IV) and starts halfway through.
Notice when “Africa” and “If I Were A Boy” enter in the Axis of Awesome medley. They start staggered from the other songs so that they line up properly.
, , , , and all use the same four chords (I-V-vi-IV), just rearranged.
On its own, I-V-vi-IV appears in only [3%] of songs, but if we count these rotations, this family of progressions shows up in [20%] of hits.
So, no, pop isn’t all axis of awesome. But there are some dominant patterns that operate in the same way.
Ok, but even if pop songs pull from a variety of progressions, perhaps each song just endlessly loops that single progression, without creativity or nuance?

text.value: If we want to count the number of progressions in a song, we should weight them by how often they appear.

We’ll call that a song’s number of effective progressions. That way, a song dominated by one progression, with a couple of others sprinkled in, scores close to 1, while a song that spreads its time across many progressions scores higher.
There’s a pretty even split between songs with few progressions and songs with a lot of progressions.
But that has changed over time.
The median song went from 4.4 effective progressions in the 1970s (the most diverse decade) to 1.9 in the 2010s (the most homogenous).
So even though it’s not the case that most songs are just 1 loop, songs are getting loopier. The Axis of Awesome boys had their finger on something real.
What about the final claim, that progressions are deployed ubiquitously across time?

text.value: The axis of awesome progression hasn’t always been a thing, it surged in the late 2000s.
This progression is [3x] more common in the 2000s compared to other decades, and was found in a full [11%] of songs.
The Axis of Awesome sketch, performed in 2009, is a product of its time period.
It begs the question: Did every decade have its own version of the axis of awesome chord progression?
Here is every decade’s signature progression, which we chose based on a combination of its prevalence and uniqueness to that decade.
The lines are all pretty flat… with one huge exception: the 50s and 60s was dominated by doo wop.
[1 in 9] songs during that period included a doo wop progression. It was [2.6x] more common then than overall in the dataset.
It’s the predecessor to axis of awesome (I-V-vi-IV), using the same chords in a slightly different order for a slightly different sound.
These two bangers dominated and defined their respective eras.
“The four chords” joke works because it’s not true, but it’s also not not true.
I-V-vi-IV on repeat works for a reason, and you can hear it and similar sounds across pop music going way back.
*WIP*
Curious what the next generation’s axis of awesome progression will be? It’s probably a tiny dot on our map right now, or maybe not even a cluster yet…
